opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, partly because I feel somewhat responsible for it. The transformer has been so successful that it's sucked all the oxygen out of the room. When one architecture works this well, all the incentives line up behind it. If you're a PhD student, a tweak to the transformer is far more likely to get published and cited than some weird new idea that doesn't beat the baseline on day one. If you're a company, you've built your whole infrastructure, your kernels, your hardware assumptions, around attention and matrix multiplies. So anything new isn't just competing with the transformer as an idea; it's competing with years of engineering and optimization.

There's also the problem that it's simply good enough. Before transformers, we had RNNs and LSTMs, and people could feel the limitations. There was a lot of pain, and pain drives exploration. Now you can just scale things up and get better results, so the pressure to look elsewhere is much weaker. And the bar has become incredibly high. A new architecture has to be not just slightly better but obviously better to justify the switching costs. That's very hard to show at small scale, and most people can't afford to test at large scale.

What worries me is that we may be stuck in a local optimum. We've basically stopped doing the broad, curiosity-driven exploration that led to the transformer in the first place. That was a small group of people with the freedom to try things that didn't obviously make sense. Today there's so much money and pressure that research has narrowed, with lots of people making incremental improvements to the same thing. That's actually part of why I wanted to step back and do something different, to create space for more open-ended research again. I'd honestly be quite happy if something came along and replaced the transformer. I think that would be a sign the field is healthy.

r002.rationale: The response describes research narrowing and less curiosity-driven exploration, but does not attribute the problem to creative talents going unused rather than lost.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I think it comes down to a few things that compound on each other.

The first one is just the practical reality of how research gets done now. The transformer has had an enormous amount of engineering effort poured into it. The kernels are optimized, the hardware is designed around it, the libraries are built for it, and everyone knows how to train it. So if you come along with a new architecture, you're not competing against the transformer as an idea, you're competing against a decade of tuning. Your new thing has to beat something that's had thousands of people hill climbing on it, and it has to do that on day one, with your one grad student and your little compute budget. That's a really unfair fight, and most of the time the new idea loses, not because it's worse, but because it's untuned.

The second thing is the incentive structure. When we did the transformer work at Google, there was a lot of freedom to just mess around. Nobody was really watching, the stakes were low, and we could try weird things. Now the field is incredibly competitive, people are under a lot of pressure to publish, and the safest way to get a paper accepted is to take the thing that works and add a small tweak that gives you a small improvement. That's a very rational thing to do for your career, but it means nobody is exploring the parts of the space that are far away from what we already have. Everyone is clustered around the same local optimum.

And then there's the scaling story, which I think has actually been a bit damaging in this respect. Once people saw that you could just make the transformer bigger and it kept getting better, the question shifted from "what's the right architecture" to "how do we get more compute." And that's a question that favours big labs and favours not changing anything, because changing the architecture is risk, and you don't want risk when you're spending a hundred million dollars on a training run.

I'll also say, honestly, I think there's something a bit uncomfortable about how much attention the transformer gets. I was there when it was made, and I can tell you it was not the product of some deep theoretical insight. It was a bunch of people trying things, and this one happened to work. There's nothing sacred about it. I'd actually be quite happy if it got replaced, and I think it's a little bit of a failure of the field that it hasn't yet.

So what do we do about it? I think you need to deliberately create spaces where people can do exploratory work without the pressure to beat state of the art immediately. That's part of what we're trying to do at Sakana, really trying to look at nature and evolution and ways of combining models that aren't just "one big model, train it harder." You need to be willing to look bad for a while. The ideas that end up mattering usually look worse than the incumbent at the start, and if your evaluation process kills everything that looks worse at the start, you'll never find them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses engineering investment in transformers and the shift toward compute, but does not say corporate AI work has shifted toward prompting foundation models.

r002.rationale: It calls for more exploratory work, but does not attribute the problem to researchers’ creative talents going unused rather than lost.

r003.rationale: It says pressure to publish makes small, safe tweaks the rational career choice and leaves researchers clustered near existing approaches instead of exploring unconventional ideas.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how research is rewarded. If you’re working on the same architecture as everyone else, you inherit all their progress—the optimizations, the infrastructure, the tricks that make training work. You can change one thing, compare it against a familiar baseline, and write a fairly clear paper.

If you try a completely different architecture, you’re giving all of that up. Your first attempt is probably going to perform worse than something thousands of people have spent years refining. And then you have to convince people that it’s worth pursuing, even though the numbers aren’t as good yet. That’s a much harder position to be in.

So I don’t think convergence necessarily tells us we’ve found the best architecture. It tells us there’s a very strong incentive to keep improving the architecture that already works. We need room for ideas to be bad initially without treating that as proof that they’re a dead end.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss researchers’ creative talents or say that they go unused rather than being lost.

r003.rationale: It says familiar architectures make it easier to write a clear paper, while unconventional approaches may perform worse and are harder to justify. This communicates how research rewards and publication prospects discourage pursuing those ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how expensive it is to try something genuinely different. If you change one component of a transformer, you’ve got a fairly good idea of how to train it and what to compare it against. If you change the whole architecture and it doesn’t work immediately, you don’t know whether the idea is bad or whether you just haven’t found the right way to train it yet.

And there’s a feedback loop there. The architecture that’s already successful gets more attention, better tooling, more people figuring out how to make it run efficiently. So it becomes an increasingly difficult baseline to compete with. You’re comparing your new idea, which you’ve spent a few weeks on, against something that the entire field has spent years optimizing.

That makes incremental work a very reasonable choice for an individual researcher. But collectively, I think we need more room for people to pursue ideas that don’t look competitive straight away.

r002.rationale: The response attributes limited architectural experimentation to cost, uncertainty, and feedback loops; it says nothing about creative talents going unused.
